content: 1. Loss to follow-up and delayed linkage to treatment were observed to be more common when Western blotting was used in HIV testing strategies. This was associated with higher costs and lower preference among both clients and healthcare providers. 2. The 2019 WHO Consolidated Guidelines on HIV Testing Services noted that the turnaround time for results was generally shorter when Western blotting was not used. Across five studies, the median turnaround time was reduced by approximately five days when testing algorithms excluded Western blotting. 3. The quality of evidence supporting these findings was rated as very low. A meta-analysis of three studies indicated that individuals tested with Western blotting were more likely to be lost to follow-up compared to those tested with alternative strategies. 4. Another meta-analysis of two studies demonstrated that a higher proportion of individuals with HIV were successfully linked to care when testing strategies excluded Western blotting. Again, the quality of evidence was very low. 5. Nine studies conducted in various countries, including Australia, Belgium, China, Malawi, and the USA, consistently reported that both patients and providers preferred HIV testing strategies that did not include Western blotting. These strategies were favored for being faster, easier to perform, and more suitable for non-clinical settings. 6. One study reported slightly higher uptake of testing using Western blotting or enzyme immunoassays compared to rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) (55% vs. 45%). However, individuals opting for RDTs were often at higher risk of HIV acquisition, such as men who have sex with men, those engaging in receptive anal sex, or those with a history of drug or alcohol use during sexual activity. 7. Four studies in the USA compared the costs and resource use of HIV testing algorithms with and without Western blotting. One study found that the higher costs associated with Western blotting were primarily driven by labor and reagent expenses, with reagent costs nearly double and labor costs more than ten times those of RDTs. 8. Overall, testing with Western blotting was found to be more than three times as expensive as testing algorithms without it. Cost savings of approximately 15% were achieved in one study by removing Western blotting from the testing algorithm. 9. HIV testing strategies without Western blotting were deemed highly feasible in many settings. These assays required less infrastructure and could be performed by a variety of healthcare workers, including trained lay providers and community health workers. 10. Implementing immediate antiretroviral therapy (ART) and streamlining pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) programs may not be feasible with Western blotting due to the longer time required to receive results. Transitioning away from Western blotting is likely to improve equity and uptake of HIV testing services, particularly among populations at high risk or those not reached by existing services. 11. The WHO Guideline Development Group (GDG) recommended against the use of Western blotting in HIV testing strategies and algorithms. This recommendation was based on evidence suggesting that Western blotting contributes to longer times to diagnosis, greater loss to follow-up, and higher costs, while being less acceptable to both providers and clients. 12. The GDG determined that the harms of using Western blotting in testing algorithms strongly outweigh the benefits. They advised the WHO to make a strong recommendation to discontinue the use of Western blotting and line immunoassays in HIV testing strategies. 13. Transitioning away from Western blotting will require national policy changes, staff training, and consultation with communities and stakeholders. Promoting the shift to faster, more accurate testing methods may increase demand for HIV testing services, particularly among key populations. 14. Verification of HIV testing algorithms is critical before widespread implementation. This ensures that the selected products work well together and do not share common false-reactive results, which could lead to misdiagnosis. 15. The accuracy of verified HIV testing algorithms should be continuously monitored through post-market surveillance and retesting of newly diagnosed individuals before initiating ART. 16. Verification studies require technical expertise and data analysis and may be conducted in laboratory or point-of-use settings. A national task force should oversee the process, including protocol adaptation, product selection, and dissemination of results. 17. The WHO recommends that HIV testing algorithms be verified prior to procurement and rollout. Properly chosen combinations of RDTs or enzyme immunoassays can provide reliable results at a lower cost. 18. Verification involves determining whether products have a high degree of shared false reactivity, which would make them unsuitable for use in the same testing algorithm. This process includes three phases prior to widespread rollout. 19. To mitigate risks of stock-outs or recalls, it is critical to select multiple products for each assay in the testing algorithm. If a new product must be introduced temporarily, re-verification of the algorithm is necessary. 20. Training of study staff is essential for verification studies. All test operators must be proficient in handling specimens, performing assays, and recording results. Accurate record-keeping and data quality practices are crucial to minimize errors. 21. Specimens for verification studies should be adequately characterized for the presence or absence of HIV. Serum or plasma is recommended for ease of handling and storage, while capillary whole blood may be used if sufficient volume can be collected. 22. The WHO strongly recommends against the use of Western blotting and line immunoassays in HIV testing strategies due to their higher costs, longer turnaround times, and lower acceptability. Transitioning to alternative testing methods is expected to improve equity, reduce costs, and enhance the overall effectiveness of HIV testing services.
